query: As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has high strength at room temperature and elevated temperature but a relatively high density of 10.21 g cm−3. What single intervention could reduce its density without sacrificing its mechanical properties at room temperature and at elevated temperatures, including approximately 1000 °C? State the proposed intervention and mechanism, predict directional changes relative to as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, define the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, identify supporting prior evidence, and propose an experiment and rejection criterion that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting Ta with Nb in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy (to form HfMoNbTiZr) will lower the overall alloy density while preserving its high strength at room temperature and at ≈1000 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr refractory high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and excellent room and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.intervention: Replace the high-density Ta in the alloy with an equimolar amount of Nb.
generation.conditions: Mechanical performance is evaluated under static tensile/compressive loads at room temperature and at elevated temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C, using alloys prepared with similar casting and homogenization processes.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a similar refractory BCC (or related) solid-solution microstructure with comparable lattice distortion and precipitation behavior to ensure strength retention.
generation.mechanism: Nb has a significantly lower density (≈8.57 g/cm³) than Ta (≈16.65 g/cm³) but can play a similar role in stabilizing the high-entropy solid solution. This substitution is expected to reduce the overall density by lowering the contribution from heavy elements while maintaining the atomic-scale lattice interactions and dislocation impediments that underpin the strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures near 1000 °C.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in overall alloy density by an estimated 5–10% with minimal (if any) degradation in tensile yield strength and creep resistance at both room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with a density of ~10.21 g/cm³ and demonstrated high strength and stability at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The performance assessment is valid for alloys processed via conventional casting and homogenization routes and tested under static loading conditions at room temperature and up to ≈1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in density and the detailed impact on microstructural evolution and mechanical properties depend on precise phase stability and atomic interactions after Nb substitution. Minor changes in yield strength or creep behavior may occur due to differences in alloying interactions that must be experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloy variants using identical processing conditions: (1) the baseline as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy and (2) the modified alloy HfMoNbTiZr where Ta is entirely replaced by Nb. Characterize both alloys using density measurements, X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analysis, and microscopy (SEM/TEM) for microstructure evaluation. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and at ~1000 °C, as well as creep tests at elevated temperatures to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile yield and ultimate strength
Phase constitution and lattice parameters via XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Nb-substituted alloy shows less than a 3% decrease in density relative to the baseline or if its mechanical performance (yield strength or creep resistance) decreases by more than 10% compared to the as-cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy, the hypothesis will be falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. By combining refractory elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, Hf, …etc. in equi- or near equi-molar ratios, several RHEAs with promising mechanical properties have been reported [5] – [7] . However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties.
